title: TAFs, GFA, and Winds Aloft Forecasts

questions.text: A pilot checks TAFs at both the departure and destination airports — both show VFR conditions. The 120-mile en route corridor has no TAF sites. Has the pilot completed an adequate weather briefing for the en route airspace under 14 CFR 91.103?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes — VFR conditions at departure and destination constitute a complete route briefing; the intervening airspace is presumed VFR unless a SIGMET or AIRMET specifically covers the corridor

options.label: B
options.text: Yes — TAFs at both endpoints bracket the route and allow the pilot to interpolate weather by assuming conditions improve or worsen linearly between the two airports over the 120-mile corridor

options.label: C
options.text: No — a TAF provides a forecast for a 5-statute-mile radius around one airport only; 14 CFR 91.103 requires obtaining weather for the route of flight, which requires a product like the GFA to evaluate en route conditions beyond TAF coverage

options.label: D
options.text: No — TAFs are never sufficient for cross-country flights regardless of distance; all cross-country planning under 14 CFR 91.103 requires a full verbal briefing from a Flight Service Station specialist

questions.explanation: A TAF covers only a 5-statute-mile radius from the airport's runway complex. The 120 miles of corridor between two airports is entirely outside the geographic validity of both TAFs. 14 CFR 91.103 requires familiarity with all available weather information 'concerning the flight' — which includes the en route airspace. The Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA), available on AviationWeather.gov, is the correct product to evaluate en route conditions. Assuming weather interpolates linearly between the two endpoints is meteorologically invalid — fronts, fog banks, and convective lines do not distribute linearly. The position that TAFs are never sufficient and that all cross-country planning requires a full verbal FSS briefing is overbroad — digital GFA and approved EFB products are fully compliant with 91.103.

questions.text: A TAF for a destination airport contains: 'FM2200 BKN008 1SM BR PROB40 TEMPO 2300/0100 VFR.' A pilot plans to arrive at 2300Z. What does this forecast tell the pilot about arrival conditions?

options.label: A
options.text: Conditions at 2300Z are forecast as IFR under FM2200 — broken ceiling at 800 AGL and 1SM in mist — with a 40-50% probability of temporary VFR recoveries between 2300Z and 0100Z

options.label: B
options.text: Conditions will be permanently VFR from 2300Z because the TEMPO group indicates the BKN008 conditions were scheduled to end at 2300Z when the TEMPO period begins

options.label: C
options.text: Conditions will be clear and VFR at 2300Z — the PROB40 TEMPO VFR group indicates that clear conditions have a 40% probability and will temporary override the BKN008 conditions from the FM group

options.label: D
options.text: No definitive forecast exists — PROB40 data is not used for operational flight planning because the FAA prohibits considering any element with less than a 50% probability during preflight evaluation

questions.explanation: The FM2200 group replaces all prior conditions with broken clouds at 800 feet AGL and 1SM visibility in mist — IFR conditions — effective at 2200Z. The PROB40 TEMPO group that follows indicates a 40-50% probability of temporary VFR conditions between 2300Z and 0100Z — brief recoveries within the dominant IFR period. The pilot planning a 2300Z arrival should treat this as an IFR arrival window with a uncertain chance of marginal VFR breaks. Treating the PROB40 TEMPO VFR group as overriding the FM base condition — concluding clear and VFR at 2300Z — inverts the relationship; PROB40 TEMPO does not override the FM base condition, it describes temporary fluctuations within it. Claiming that PROB40 data cannot be used for operational flight planning incorrectly characterizes its regulatory status — while PROB30 cannot be used for IFR alternate planning, PROB40 conditions are operationally significant for VFR planning evaluation.

questions.text: The Winds Aloft forecast for a station at 2,000 feet MSL elevation shows no wind or temperature data for the 3,000-foot level. A pilot needs winds at 3,000 MSL (1,000 feet AGL) for a low-altitude leg. Why is the data missing?

options.label: A
options.text: The NWS does not forecast winds below 6,000 feet MSL for any station in the CONUS network because boundary layer turbulence invalidates all model output below that altitude

options.label: B
options.text: The Winds Aloft forecast includes data for every 1,000-foot level, so if 3,000-foot MSL data is absent, the FSS station had a sensor malfunction during the forecast production cycle and data should be requested via phone

options.label: C
options.text: Winds at 3,000 feet MSL are only available for stations above 1,500 feet MSL elevation on the West Coast; all other stations in the forecast network require minimum 6,000 MSL for initial forecast data

options.label: D
options.text: Winds are not forecast within 1,500 feet of station elevation — at 2,000 feet MSL station elevation, forecasting winds at 3,000 MSL (1,000 AGL) falls within the exclusion zone, and temperatures are also excluded within 2,500 feet of station elevation

questions.explanation: The Winds Aloft (FB) forecast has two altitude exclusion rules: (1) Wind data is not forecast within 1,500 feet above station elevation — because surface effects make the boundary layer forecast unreliable. (2) Temperature data is not forecast within 2,500 feet above station elevation. For a station at 2,000 feet MSL, the wind exclusion floor is 3,500 feet MSL (2,000 + 1,500). Data at 3,000 MSL is within the exclusion zone for this station. Additionally, the 3,000-foot MSL level carries no temperature data for any station in the forecast network. The pilot should use the next available level above the exclusion zone or contact FSS for supplemental low-altitude wind information.

questions.text: A Winds Aloft forecast encodes winds at FL180 as '7504+20.' What do these values decode to?

options.label: A
options.text: Wind from 075° True at 4 knots, temperature +20°C — standard format where the first two digits are direction in tens of degrees and the next two digits are speed

options.label: B
options.text: Wind from 250° True at 4 knots, temperature +20°C — standard format reading the direction as written minus 50 because all FL180 and above forecasts adjust magnetic variation by subtracting 50 from the heading

options.label: C
options.text: Wind from 075° True at 104 knots, temperature +20°C — a high-speed jet stream wind where only the speed is adjusted by adding 100 knots to the encoded value without modifying the reported direction

options.label: D
options.text: Wind from 250° True at 104 knots, temperature +20°C — high wind encoding where the direction exceeds 36 tens-of-degrees, requiring subtraction of 50 from direction (75-50=25=250°) and addition of 100 to speed (04+100=104 knots)

questions.explanation: When the Winds Aloft speed code shows direction digits exceeding 36 (the maximum compass tens-of-degrees), the high wind encoding is active: subtract 50 from the direction digits and add 100 to the speed digits. For '7504': 75 - 50 = 25 → 250° True direction. 04 + 100 = 104 knots. Temperature +20°C. This typically occurs at jet stream altitudes (FL180 and above) where winds routinely exceed 100 knots. Reading the raw code as 075° True at 4 knots skips the high-wind decode entirely, producing physically implausible 4-knot jet stream winds. Decoding it as 075° True at 104 knots applies the speed correction but not the direction correction. Decoding it as 250° True at 4 knots applies the direction correction but misidentifies the speed as 4 knots.

questions.text: A pilot during a checkride oral references 'the area forecast' to explain how they evaluated en route weather between two airports for a 2026 flight. What is the most accurate DPE response to this reference?

options.label: A
options.text: The reference is partially acceptable — the Area Forecast was discontinued in the western states but continues to be issued daily for the eastern CONUS by the Miami and Atlanta Aviation Weather Centers

options.label: B
options.text: The reference is acceptable if supplemented — the Area Forecast is still published but only as an archived 6-hour product that must be combined with a current SIGMET to constitute an adequate en route weather assessment

options.label: C
options.text: The reference reveals outdated training — the text-based Area Forecast (FA) was retired and replaced by the Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA) in 2017; the applicant should reference the GFA for current en route weather evaluation

options.label: D
options.text: The reference is appropriate — the Area Forecast remains an active FAA weather product, serving as the text-based en route weather evaluation tool for IFR flights while the GFA is reserved for VFR planning

questions.explanation: The NWS retired the text-based Area Forecast (FA) for the contiguous United States in 2017 and replaced it with the Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA), accessible through AviationWeather.gov. An applicant who references 'the area forecast' in 2026 is demonstrating training from materials that are nine years out of date — a red flag for the DPE regarding the quality of the applicant's overall weather education. The correct term is the GFA (Graphical Forecasts for Aviation). All other options describe operational states of the Area Forecast that have not existed since 2017.

questions.text: The Winds Aloft forecast encodes the 6,000-foot level as '9900+10.' What conditions does this indicate?

options.label: A
options.text: Wind from 990° True at 0 knots — an instrument malfunction code indicating the directional sensor at the 6,000-foot forecast level has reported an invalid heading value out of the 360-degree compass range

options.label: B
options.text: Calm winds (less than 5 knots, direction variable) with a temperature of +10°C — the '9900' code is the standard Winds Aloft designation for light and variable winds under 5 knots at this level

options.label: C
options.text: Wind from 990° True at 0 knots and temperature +10°C — a rare high-altitude jet stream condition where the Coriolis force causes winds to appear to originate from a bearing greater than 360 degrees at elevation

options.label: D
options.text: Wind from 099° True at 0 knots and temperature +10°C — the 9900 coding means the wind is from the east at precisely 099° but with no measurable speed because the anemometer reported calm conditions

questions.explanation: In Winds Aloft forecasts, the code '9900' is the designated indicator for calm or light and variable winds — defined as less than 5 knots with no dominant direction. No compass heading is given because the wind is insufficiently steady to assign a direction. The '+10' suffix indicates a temperature of +10°C at that level. This code frequently appears in high-pressure centers or during very light wind conditions at lower altitudes. Reading '9900' as a sensor malfunction code fabricates a designation that does not exist. Reading '9900' as a direction (099°) correctly takes the '00' as zero speed but applies an invalid direction interpretation. Reading it as a rare jet stream condition — the Coriolis force making winds appear to originate from a bearing greater than 360° — invents a meteorological condition that does not exist.

questions.text: You are briefing for a 150-mile VFR cross-country. Both TAFs show VFR conditions. The GFA shows a band of MVFR conditions — ceilings around 1,200 AGL with mist — crossing your route about 60 miles from departure. It is forecast to clear two hours after your planned departure. What is the SAFEST action?

options.label: A
options.text: Delay departure by at least two hours to allow the MVFR band to clear, confirm with an updated GFA and METARs from stations along the route that conditions have improved, then depart when VFR is confirmed across the corridor

options.label: B
options.text: Depart and plan to divert around the MVFR band when you see it visually from the air — maintaining visual contact with the ground while flying under the mist layer is legal in Class G airspace and represents valid VFR risk management

options.label: C
options.text: Cancel the flight completely — any GFA showing MVFR conditions within 100 miles of a planned route constitutes an automatic no-go condition under FAA ADM standards regardless of current TAF readings

options.label: D
options.text: Depart on schedule — the GFA is a model-based probabilistic tool with low accuracy at the local level; the VFR TAFs at both airports are more reliable and the MVFR band may dissipate faster than forecast

questions.explanation: A GFA showing MVFR conditions with 1,200 AGL ceilings and mist at a point 60 miles along your route is operationally disqualifying for a VFR crossing without current confirmation that conditions have cleared. The TAFs do not cover en route airspace — this is precisely the scenario the GFA was designed to reveal. The correct action is to delay until the forecast clearing has occurred, then verify independently with current METARs from nearby stations and updated GFA before departing. Departing on schedule by dismissing the GFA as inaccurate to rationalize departure is Macho. Choosing to depart and divert around the band only when you see it from the air is Get-There-Itis — the phrase 'plan to divert when I see it' means departing without a plan, which is the hallmark of get-there-itis ADM. Flying under a mist layer at 1,200 AGL near obstacles is not safe risk management. Cancelling the flight completely is Resignation — MVFR conditions forecast to clear in 2 hours warrant a delay, not cancellation.
questions.sjt_rationale: Dismissing the GFA to depart is Macho — discounting a valid forecast tool to avoid changing plans. Diverting only when the band is seen from the air is Get-There-Itis — departing into known marginal conditions with a reactive (not proactive) weather strategy. Cancelling outright is Resignation — treating a temporary condition as permanent. Delaying to confirm is professional ADM: delay, verify update, confirm before departing.

questions.text: The destination TAF contains 'PROB40 TEMPO 1800/2000 BKN005 1/2SM TSRA' and your planned arrival is at 1850Z. Conditions are currently VFR. A passenger has a connecting flight they cannot miss. What is the SAFEST decision?

options.label: A
options.text: Depart immediately but ask ATC for an expedited routing to arrive well before 1800Z — arriving 45 minutes early eliminates the TEMPO risk window and the passenger obligation is preserved without compromising safety

options.label: B
options.text: Evaluate the connecting flight as an external pressure factor, assess whether a one-hour delay would allow the TEMPO window to close, plan a divert alternate with maintained VFR approach capability, and decline departure if no safe margin exists even if the passenger misses their connection

options.label: C
options.text: Cancel the flight — the FAA defines any PROB40 TEMPO condition as disqualifying for VFR flight at the destination regardless of the actual probability, making departure illegal under 14 CFR 91.103

options.label: D
options.text: Depart — PROB40 means only a 40-50% chance; you are more likely to arrive in VFR than not, and the brief TEMPO window means any thunderstorm would be short-lived and likely passed by the time you arrive at 1850Z

questions.explanation: A PROB40 TEMPO for thunderstorm conditions (BKN005 = ceiling 500 AGL, 1/2SM in heavy rain during a thunderstorm) during your planned 1850Z arrival window is operationally serious — this represents potentially unlandable conditions for a VFR aircraft. The correct response is a structured decision: (1) identify the external pressure (passenger connecting flight — the 'E' in PAVE); (2) evaluate whether a 1–2 hour delay would allow the TEMPO window to close at 2000Z; (3) identify a divert alternate with confirmed VFR; (4) make the decision free from the passenger pressure. If no safe margin exists — no alternate, time constraint forces arrival during TSRA — the flight should not depart regardless of the passenger's itinerary. Departing because the probability seems favorable is Invulnerability — using probability math to rationalize exposure to a thunderstorm arrival. PROB40 TEMPO does not guarantee 60% clear — it may be 100% thunderstorm that specific day. Departing and asking for expedited routing to beat the arrival window is Get-There-Itis — trying to outrun the weather to preserve the schedule. Cancelling on the belief that PROB40 TEMPO is an automatic regulatory no-go misstates the regulatory status of PROB40 — it is not an automatic no-go by regulation, but it demands careful evaluation.
questions.sjt_rationale: Departing on favorable odds is Invulnerability — rationalizing a thunderstorm arrival gamble with favorable odds. Departing with an expedited routing to beat the window is Get-There-Itis — restructuring the flight to serve the schedule rather than safety. Cancelling outright is Resignation — misapplying a non-existent legal prohibition as an excuse to cancel rather than evaluate. Evaluating PAVE, weighing the delay, planning an alternate, and accepting the result regardless of passenger pressure is the professional ADM response.
